title: Synthetic polymers
learningObjective: know that an addition polymer is formed by joining up many small molecules called monomers; understand how to draw the repeat unit of an addition polymer, including poly(ethene), poly(propene), poly(chloroethene) and (poly)tetrafluoroethene; understand how to deduce the structure of a monomer from the repeat unit of an addition polymer and vice versa; explain problems in the disposal of addition polymers, including: • their inertness and inability to biodegrade • the production of toxic gases when they are burned.; know that condensation polymerisation, in which a dicarboxylic acid reacts with a diol, produces a polyester and water; understand how to write the structural and displayed formula of a polyester, showing the repeat unit, given the formulae of the monomers from which it is formed including the reaction of ethanedioic acid and ethanediol:; know that some polyesters, known as biopolyesters, are biodegradable

sections.title: Synthetic polymers
sections.markdown:
A [[polymer]] is a giant molecule built by joining huge numbers of
small units together, and once you know what to look for you will
find them everywhere: polymers are large molecules consisting
of many repeating units, and this chapter looks at two
different ways that polymers can be made. Natural polymers run
your body and your
kitchen: proteins are polypeptides, and sugar is built from
polysaccharides — chains you have already met in biology.
Synthetic polymers run everything else: plastic bags, clothing,
water pipes, non-stick pans. This lesson is about the synthetic
kind, and it turns on one idea — a [[polymer]] grows from small
starting molecules called [[monomer]]s, and there are exactly two
ways the joining can happen. **[[addition-polymerisation]]** builds
polymers such as poly(ethene) and PVC: the monomers simply add on,
one after another, and nothing is thrown away. **[[condensation-polymerisation]]**
builds a [[polyester]]: two different monomers
alternate down the chain, and each time a pair joins, a small
molecule is expelled. Everything in this chapter hangs off that
one distinction.

The specification splits this lesson down the same line, and the
split decides which exam paper each half belongs to. Four
statements are for everyone: knowing that an addition polymer is
formed by joining up many small molecules called [[monomer]]s
(4.44); drawing repeat units for the four named polymers
(4.45); deducing a monomer from a repeat unit and back again
(4.46); and explaining the disposal problems (4.47). Three more
statements carry the C suffix — condensation polymerisation
(4.48C), writing a polyester's structural and displayed formula
(4.49C), and biodegradable polyesters (4.50C) — and C-suffixed
content is chemistry-only: it appears on Paper 2C, not on the
double-award papers. If you sit Paper 1C only, the addition half
of this lesson is your whole territory; the condensation half is
flagged as you enter it.

The route through the chapter follows the chemistry. First the
addition story: how a C=C double bond opens out and chains grow,
what a repeat unit is, and how to write the polymerisation
reaction starting from *any* alkene — ethene, propene,
chloroethene and tetrafluoroethene in turn. Then the reverse
skill: given a polymer's structure, work backwards to the monomer
that built it. Then the bill that polymers present to the
environment, because their great strength — inertness — is
exactly what makes their disposal a problem. Finally the
condensation story: a diol and a dicarboxylic acid joining
with water expelled, the [[polyester]] family, and the
biodegradable members that might solve the disposal problem the
addition polymers created.

:::prior-knowledge
Three ideas load this lesson. First, the alkenes and their C=C
double bond — the reactive site every addition polymer grows
from — including the bromine-water test that spotlights that
bond (u4:c25). Second, cracking, the source of the small alkene
molecules that feed polymer production (u4:c23). Third, the
ester group –COO– and the condensation reaction that builds it
(u4:c28): the condensation half of this lesson reuses that exact
group, just at every junction of a chain instead of once in a
small molecule. If the alkenes feel shaky, repair them first —
every polymer in the addition half is an alkene in disguise.
:::

:::exam-hint
Statement 4.44 says *know* — a recall item — while 4.45 and 4.46
say *understand*, which means drawn structures, not sentences.
Notice also how the C suffix sorts the paper route: 4.48C,
4.49C and 4.50C are the only statements in this chapter that
name condensation chemistry, so if the question number carries
a C, the answer lives in the second half of this lesson. Asking
yourself "which paper is this on?" before revising is a cheap
way to prioritise.
:::

:::misconception
"Polymers are a synthetic invention — chemistry made them and
chemistry owns them." Chemistry certainly perfected them, but
nature got there first and at enormous scale: the protein
chains in your hair and muscles are polypeptides, and starch
is a polysaccharide. Natural and synthetic polymers are built
on the same idea — many repeating units joined into one giant
molecule — and the only thing this lesson adds is the two
industrial routes for doing the joining.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you define a [[polymer]] as a giant molecule of many
repeating units and give one natural and one synthetic example?
Can you name the two polymerisation routes and the small
molecule each one expels (or does not)? Can you say which three
specification statements of this chapter are Paper 2C only? If
yes, the addition half is ready to open.
:::

sections.title: Addition polymerisation
sections.markdown:
Ethene is the smallest alkene and the smallest hydrocarbon that
carries a carbon–carbon double bond, and it is produced by
cracking longer fractions (u4:c23). That double bond is the whole
story of this section. You can represent an ethene molecule as
the molecular formula C₂H₄, as the displayed formula with all
four bonds drawn, or as a ball-and-stick model — three views of
the same pair of carbon atoms joined by two pairs of shared
electrons.

Under the right conditions, molecules carrying C=C bonds join
together into very long chains. Part of each double bond breaks
to become a single bond, and the electrons set free are used to
grip the next molecule in line. Heat, high pressure and an
[[initiator]] start the process, and the molecules add on and on:
lots of little molecules called [[monomer]]s join into one big
molecule called a [[polymer]]. Nothing else is formed and
nothing is lost — the monomers simply add onto each other — and
that is why the process is called [[addition-polymerisation]].
With ethene as the monomer the product is [[polyethene]], more
usually called polythene. The chains are not all the same
length: a typical chain carries somewhere between about 4000 and
40 000 carbon atoms, all stitched together by the same reaction.

:::key-point
An [[initiator]] is used to start the process. You mustn't call
it a catalyst because it is consumed in the reaction — bits of
it end up bonded onto the ends of every chain. Catalysts, like
the concentrated sulfuric acid in esterification (u4:c28), come
out unchanged; an initiator does not.
:::

For exam purposes the reaction is written with displayed
formulae. The monomer's double bond opens out into a single
bond, the two freed bonds become continuation bonds, and the
whole arrangement sits inside square brackets with a subscript
n:

```
   H  H                H  H
   |  |                |  |
n  C=C      →        [ C-C ]          (continued on both sides)
   |  |                |  |
   H  H                H  H
```

The structure inside the brackets is called the [[repeat-unit]],
and n is simply a large but variable number — the repeat unit
repeats many times down the chain. Draw the bonds on the two
sides of the bracket extending *outside* it: those are the
continuation bonds that connect each unit to the next ones in
the chain. The equation reads "n ethene molecules give one
poly(ethene) molecule", and it is balanced in the most
satisfying way — n C₂H₄ on the left, (C₂H₄)ₙ on the right, every
atom accounted for because nothing was lost.

:::key-point
Although the polymer is called poly(ethene), it is actually an alkane-like structure: the polymer is [[saturated]] and will
not decolourise bromine water. The double bond each monomer
brought to the reaction is spent in the joining — the polymer
chain carries only single bonds, so the alkene test that works
on ethene (u4:c25) is silent on poly(ethene).
:::

Poly(ethene) comes in two grades. Low-density poly(ethene),
LDPE, is mainly used as a thin film for polythene bags: very
flexible, not very strong. High-density poly(ethene), HDPE, is
used where greater strength and rigidity are needed — plastic
bottles such as milk bottles. The recycling symbols on the
bottom of packaging tell you which you are holding: the letters
HDPE next to the recycling mark mean high-density
poly(ethene), and any other letters mean some other polymer
entirely. A curiosity worth knowing from the extension of the
chain-ends story: polymer chains do not end tidily — bits of
the initiator stay bonded on at either end, but for
International GCSE you never need to draw them.

:::exam-hint
When you draw an addition polymerisation reaction, never change
anything except opening out the double bond and drawing the
continuation bonds on each side. The two classic lost marks:
forgetting the subscript n after the bracket, and hiding the
continuation bonds inside the brackets instead of letting them
cross the bracket walls.
:::

:::misconception
"Poly(ethene) has C=C bonds because it is made from ethene."
The joining consumes every double bond — that is the addition.
The polymer is [[saturated]], closer in character to an alkane
than to the alkene it came from, which is exactly why bromine
water stays orange in it. If a question shows you a polymer
fragment that still contains C=C, you are looking at the
monomer or at an unfinished drawing, not at a correct repeat
unit.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you state what an [[initiator]] does and why it is not a
catalyst? Can you draw the [[polyethene]] equation with the
[[repeat-unit]] in brackets, continuation bonds crossing the
bracket walls and the subscript n in place? Can you explain why
the polymer will not decolourise bromine water? If yes, you are
ready to run the same reaction on any alkene.
:::

sections.title: How to deduce the polymerisation reaction for any alkene
sections.markdown:
The ethene reaction is one instance of a method that works for
*any* alkene, and the method is worth learning as a drawing
routine. Always draw the alkene with the C=C vertical in the
middle. Cut the double bond into two single bonds, one on each
side. Attach a continuation bond to each freed end, wrap the
whole unit in square brackets with the subscript n, and you
have the polymerisation equation. Nothing else in the molecule
moves: whatever atoms or groups hang off the double-bond
carbons keep their positions, they just ride along on the
outside of the [[repeat-unit]].

**Propene** is the first rehearsal. Its formula is normally
written CH₃CH=CH₂ — three carbon atoms, think of it as a
modified ethene molecule with a CH₃ group attached in place of
one hydrogen atom. Run the routine: the double bond opens, the
CH₃ group stays attached to its carbon, and the product is
[[polypropene]], which used to be called polypropylene:

```
   CH₃  H               CH₃  H
   |    |               |    |
n  C == C     →       [  C - C  ]n
   |    |               |    |
   H    H               H    H
   (propene)        (poly(propene) repeat unit)
```

Poly(propene) is somewhat stronger than poly(ethene), which is
why it turns up where a bit of muscle is needed — ropes and
crates among many other things. Packaging carrying a recycling
mark with the letters PP in it or near it is made of
poly(propene).

**Chloroethene** is the second rehearsal: one of ethene's
hydrogen atoms is replaced by a chlorine, giving CH₂=CHCl. It
was once called vinyl chloride, and polymerising it gives
[[polychloroethene]] — better known by its old name,
polyvinylchloride, or PVC:

```
   Cl   H               Cl   H
   |    |               |    |
n  C == C     →       [  C - C  ]n
   |    |               |    |
   H    H               H    H
(chloroethene)   (poly(chloroethene) repeat unit)
```

Whether you draw the chlorine on the left-hand carbon or the
right-hand one makes no difference — the repeat unit is the
same either way, so pick one and stay consistent.

PVC has a lot of uses because it starts out quite strong and
rigid: water pipes and replacement windows are its natural
territory. It can also be made flexible by adding
[[plasticiser]]s — additives that slip between the chains and
let them slide — which opens up a second life for the polymer
in sheet floor coverings, and even clothing. One more property
lands it a third job: these polymers do not conduct
electricity, therefore PVC is used for electrical insulation,
the coating on the wires behind your walls.

:::exam-hint
Statement 4.45 names the four polymers whose repeat units you
must be able to draw: poly(ethene), poly(propene),
poly(chloroethene) and poly(tetrafluoroethene). Practise the
four as a set — they are the same routine run four times, with
H, CH₃, Cl and F riding on the repeat unit respectively. The
styrene case in the question bank (u4:c29:s09) is the same
routine with a whole benzene ring riding along, which is why
examiners like it: it tests the routine, not the memory.
:::

:::misconception
"The chlorine atom must be drawn on a particular side of the
repeat unit, otherwise the polymer is wrong." Addition
polymerisation leaves the substituent where the monomer had it,
and the monomer can approach the growing chain from either
end — so left and right placements describe the same polymer.
What *would* be wrong is moving the chlorine onto a hydrogen
position, dropping it entirely, or bonding it into the chain:
the substituent hangs off the carbon, never in the backbone.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you run the four-step routine (draw the alkene with C=C in
the middle, open the bond, add continuation bonds, bracket with
n) for propene and chloroethene without looking? Can you name
the polymer and one use for each? Can you explain what
[[plasticiser]]s change about PVC and why that matters for
floor coverings? If yes, the only named polymer left is the
fluorine one — next section.
:::

sections.title: The polymerisation of tetrafluoroethene
sections.markdown:
Tetrafluoroethene completes the set: it is another molecule
derived from ethene, this time with all four hydrogen atoms
replaced by fluorine, giving CF₂=CF₂. Polymerising it gives
[[ptfe]] — poly(tetrafluoroethene) — more commonly known as
Teflon. The reaction is exactly the same shape as the
poly(ethene) equation, and if you look at the two side by side
you can see it is the same reaction except that each H has been
replaced by an F:

```
   F    F               F    F
   |    |               |    |
n  C == C     →       [  C - C  ]n
   |    |               |    |
   F    F               F    F
(tetrafluoroethene)  (poly(tetrafluoroethene) repeat unit)
```

The fluorine atoms are not decoration — they are the reason
PTFE is worth its place on the specification. Carbon–fluorine
bonds are very strong, and a chain sheathed in them is
extremely unreactive. That unreactivity is the property behind
every use: PTFE is the non-stick coating on pots and pans,
where nothing bonds to the surface and nothing burns onto it,
and it lines containers for corrosive chemicals precisely
because the chemicals cannot attack it. The same inertness
returns in the disposal section (4.47) — remember it when the
question asks why polymers are a problem in landfill.

:::exam-hint
4.45 asks for the repeat unit, so learn the four named
polymers as one family of drawings: H/H for poly(ethene), CH₃/H
for poly(propene), Cl/H for poly(chloroethene), F/F for PTFE.
The F/F case is the easiest to draw and the easiest to forget
— two fluorines on each carbon, nothing else. If asked for the
[[monomer]] of PTFE, reverse the routine: put the C=C double
bond back between the two carbons of the repeat unit and you
have tetrafluoroethene, CF₂=CF₂.
:::

:::misconception
"Fluorine is ferociously reactive, so a fluorine-containing
polymer must be too." The reactivity of the element and the
reactivity of the bond are different questions. Fluorine gas
attacks almost everything, but once a C–F bond has formed it
is one of the strongest single bonds carbon makes, and a chain
of them is what makes PTFE slippery and chemically lazy. The
polymer's inertness is a property of its strong bonds, not an
echo of its elements.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you write the formula of the [[monomer]] tetrafluoroethene
and draw its polymerisation equation with the repeat unit in
brackets? Can you name the polymer, its common trade name, and
two uses? Can you explain the property that makes those uses
possible in one sentence about bonds? If yes, the addition
drawing set is complete and the backwards skill is next.
:::

sections.title: Working out the monomer for a given addition polymer
sections.markdown:
In an exam you may be handed the structure of a polymer and
asked to deduce what the [[repeat-unit]] is, or what
[[monomer]] it was made from — the skill of 4.46 running the
drawing routine of the last three sections backwards. The
method has two moves. First, find the repeat unit: take any
two adjacent carbon atoms in the main polymer chain, and the
fragment between them (plus whatever hangs off those carbons)
is the repeat unit. Second, derive the monomer: put a double
bond back between those two middle carbon atoms and get rid of
the continuation bonds. Work from the structure you are given,
and do not be distracted by how complicated the attached
groups look — they simply ride along.

:::worked-example
A short length of poly(styrene) is drawn as a carbon chain
carrying alternating hydrogens and C₆H₅ groups. Find the
repeat unit and the monomer.

Step 1 — pick two adjacent carbons in the main chain. Take a
carbon bearing H and its neighbour bearing C₆H₅: the fragment
–CH₂–CH(C₆H₅)– is the repeat unit. (Any adjacent pair gives
the same answer — the chain is the same unit repeated, so
where you start does not matter.)

Step 2 — put the double bond back between those two carbons
and remove the continuation bonds: C₆H₅CH=CH₂, which is
styrene. The C₆H₅ group is complicated to draw, but you never
need to unpack it — it came through the reaction unchanged,
and it goes back into the monomer unchanged.

Check by running the forward routine: styrene with the C=C
opened out, continuation bonds added, bracketed with n — the
poly(styrene) structure returns.
:::

The same walk answers the reverse question with equal speed:
given a monomer, open its double bond and bracket the result,
and you have the polymer. Monomer to polymer and polymer to
monomer are one routine read in two directions, and 4.46 is
satisfied by both. The benzene-ring case is the examiners'
favourite because it looks harder than it is — the ring is
just a passenger, exactly as the CH₃, Cl and F were on the
polymers of the previous sections.

:::exam-hint
The most common error in this question type is anchoring the
repeat unit on the wrong pair of carbons — picking two carbons
that are *not* adjacent, or spanning across the unit
boundary. If your derived monomer does not have its double
bond between two carbons that each carried chain bonds, your
pair was wrong: slide along by one carbon and try again. A
correct answer always re-polymerises cleanly by the forward
routine.
:::

:::misconception
"There is exactly one correct place to cut the chain, and if
you start somewhere else you get a different monomer." The
repeat unit repeats — that is the definition — so every
adjacent pair of chain carbons yields the same fragment. What
*is* fixed is the double bond's final position: it must sit
between the two carbons that were joined through the chain.
Cut anywhere, but always rebuild the C=C across the cut.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you state the two moves of the backwards routine in one
sentence each? Can you take a drawn repeat unit and restore
its [[monomer]] by re-forming the double bond? Can you explain
why any two adjacent chain carbons give the same
[[repeat-unit]]? If yes, both directions of 4.46 are yours,
and the next section turns from how polymers are made to what
happens when we are finished with them.
:::

sections.title: Disposal of addition polymers
sections.markdown:
Recycling plastics matters for two reasons at once: to save raw
materials, and because it takes a very long time for addition
polymers like poly(ethene) and poly(chloroethene) to break down
in the environment. The reason is the chemistry you have just
learned. Their chains are built from strong covalent bonds,
making them essentially inert at ordinary temperatures, and
they are [[non-biodegradable]] — they cannot be broken down by
bacteria in the environment. The very stability that makes a
water pipe last decades makes a plastic bag last
geological-looking timescales, and the same [[polymer]] chains
that refused to react with corrosive chemicals (s04) refuse
equally to react with the enzymes of decay.

One solution is to bury the problem: [[landfill]] sites are
basically just big holes in the ground where plastic waste
will remain unchanged for thousands of years. The other
widely used solution is to burn it: some countries, including
Denmark and Japan, [[incineration]] plastics to
tackle the disposal problem at scale. Burning releases a lot
of heat energy, which can be used to generate electricity —
waste as a fuel. However, there are problems associated with
this: carbon dioxide is produced, which contributes to global
warming, and toxic gases are also released, including carbon
monoxide and hydrogen chloride. The hydrogen chloride comes
from chlorine-bearing polymers — PVC is the everyday example
you met in the previous section — so the cleaner the flame,
the cleaner the chemistry, and chlorine-containing plastics
are the worst offenders in an incinerator.

:::key-point
There are advantages and disadvantages to using either method
to dispose of plastics, and the exam wants both sides of both
columns. [[landfill]]: no greenhouse gases or toxic gases
produced from the plastics, and it is cheap — but the sites
are ugly, smelly and noisy, nobody wants to live next to one,
they use large areas of land, and the waste will be there for
thousands of years. [[incineration]]: it requires little
space and can produce heat for local homes and offices or
electricity — but the plant is expensive to build and
maintain, burning produces greenhouse gases, it releases
toxic gases, and the ash produced must still be disposed of
in landfill sites.
:::

Read that table as the chemistry argument it is. Incineration
converts one waste problem (space) into an emissions problem
(CO₂ plus toxic gases), and even its ash — the incombustible
residue — ends up back in landfill, only concentrated. Neither
route destroys the polymer problem, because neither route
touches the property that causes it: the strong covalent
bonds that make addition polymers inert. That is the honest
conclusion of 4.47, and it is why the condensation polymers
later in this lesson — and their biodegradable cousins in
particular — are worth the chemistry they are getting.

:::exam-hint
Statement 4.47 asks you to *explain* the disposal problems,
"including" two named items: the inertness and inability to
biodegrade, and the production of toxic gases when they are
burned. Both words in the first item carry marks — strong
covalent bonds explain the inertness, and the inertness is why
bacteria cannot break them down. For the second item, name the
gases (carbon monoxide and hydrogen chloride) rather than just
saying "toxic gases". "Include" means the list is not
exhaustive — landfill space and ash disposal are fair extra
marks.
:::

:::misconception
"Plastic eventually rots away like paper or food — it just
takes a bit longer." Biodegrading is not slow rotting; it is
bacteria digesting a material, and bacteria can only digest
what their enzymes can attack. Paper is cellulose, a natural
polymer that evolved alongside the organisms that eat it.
Addition polymers are new, inert, and built from strong
covalent bonds nothing in a bacterium's toolkit can cut — so
they do not rot slowly, they simply persist unchanged.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you explain, in terms of bonds, why addition polymers are
[[non-biodegradable]]? Can you give one advantage and one
disadvantage each for [[landfill]] and [[incineration]]? Can
you name the two toxic gases released when plastics burn and
say which everyday polymer supplies the chlorine? If yes, the
disposal bill is understood — and the condensation half of
this lesson, where a partial answer to the problem is being
built, is next.
:::

sections.title: Condensation polymerisation
sections.markdown:
This section crosses the flag: from here to the end of the
chapter the content is chemistry-only, examined on Paper 2C
(4.48C onwards). The chemistry itself is a contrast study.
When ethene molecules combine to make a chain, the double
bonds break and the monomers just add onto each other —
nothing is lost, which is why the first half of this lesson is
called addition. Making a [[polyester]] is different. Instead
of one type of monomer, you often have two, joining
together alternately, and each time two monomers combine a
small molecule such as water or hydrogen chloride is lost. The
elimination of water gives the name [[condensation-polymerisation]]
to this type of polymerisation: a dicarboxylic acid reacts
with a diol, and the products are a polyester and water
(4.48C). It is the same condensation idea you met when an
alcohol and a carboxylic acid built an ester and expelled
water (u4:c28) — now run along a whole chain instead of once.

Draw the general reaction as a block diagram and the pattern
becomes visible. One monomer is a dicarboxylic acid — think of
it as a blue box with reactive –COOH groups at both ends. The
other is a diol — a red box with –OH groups at both ends. Line
them up and join them: at every junction an –OH and a
–COOH meet, water is removed, and an ester group forms in its
place. The chain can continue at both ends, so the boxes
alternate — acid, alcohol, acid, alcohol — with an ester group
at every seam. That repeating seam is the [[ester-link]], the
same –COO– arrangement that defined the esters of the previous
lesson (u4:c28), now repeated all the way down the polymer.

:::key-point
One of the monomers is a [[diol]]: an alcohol molecule with
one –OH at each end. Ethane-1,2-diol has the structural
formula CH₂OHCH₂OH — the prefix 'eth' says two carbon atoms,
the code 'di' says two –OH groups, and the number '1,2' says
they sit on carbons 1 and 2, one on each carbon.
Propane-1,3-diol, CH₂OHCH₂CH₂OH, has one more carbon in the
chain. And it is not a mistake that an extra 'e' appears in
these names: we talk about propan-1-ol but propane-1,3-diol.
:::

The second monomer is a [[dicarboxylic-acid]]: a carboxylic
molecule with one –COOH at each end. Ethanedioic acid has the
structural formula HOOCCOOH — two carboxylic acid groups
back to back. A more complicated example is hexane-1,6-dioic
acid, HOOCCH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂COOH, where 'hex' indicates six carbon
atoms in the main chain and '1,6-dioic acid' means two
carboxylic acid groups at either end of the molecule, on
carbons 1 and 6.

Under the right conditions, diol and dicarboxylic molecules
join together with the loss of a molecule of water each time a
new bond is formed. Both monomers react at each end, so the
joining continues at both ends of the growing chain, producing
a long-chain [[polyester]] held together by a large number of
ester groups. It does not matter whether you take the OH from
the dicarboxylic acid and the H from the alcohol or the other
way around — the polymer formed is still the same. A useful
way to practise: think of one monomer as a red rectangle with
an –OH at each end and the other as a blue rectangle with a
–COOH at each end, draw those end groups as displayed
formulae, line the rectangles up, remove the water between
them, and slot the remainder together. It looks difficult
because it is unfamiliar; a few runs and it becomes routine.

For the ethanedioic acid and ethane-1,2-diol pair, the repeat
unit and the balanced equation are:

```
n HOOC–COOH + n HO–CH₂CH₂–OH  →  –[ OC–CO–O–CH₂CH₂–O ]n–  +  2n H₂O
    (ethanedioic      (ethane-1,2-     (the polyester        (water)
      acid)             diol)          repeat unit)
```

Balance check per repeat: the monomers supply C₂H₂O₄ +
C₂H₆O₂ = C₄H₈O₆; the repeat unit carries C₄H₄O₄ and two water
molecules carry H₄O₂ — carbon, hydrogen and oxygen all
accounted for. The block-diagram version of the same reaction
works for any polyester: put real carbons and hydrogens into
the boxes — hexane-1,6-dioic acid and ethane-1,2-diol, for
example — and the identical remove-water logic builds the
identical alternating chain. One refinement for the curious:
the equation balances with 2n water molecules, but a real
chain of finite length forms only (2n – 1) of them, because
one –OH and one –COOH are left dangling at the chain's ends.

:::exam-hint
4.49C asks for the structural and displayed formula of a
polyester repeat unit, given the monomers. Draw the ester
groups *inside* the brackets and let the continuation bonds
pass through the oxygen ends: –[OC–CO–O–CH₂CH₂–O]n–. The two
classic errors are closing the chain into a ring (forgetting
the continuation bonds) and drawing an –COOH group inside the
unit — the water has already been expelled, so the unit
contains ester links, not acid groups.
:::

:::misconception
"Condensation polymerisation is just addition polymerisation
with extra steps — the products are the same kind of polymer."
The two are distinguishable at a glance, and the discriminator
is the small molecule. Addition: one monomer type, double bond
opened, nothing expelled. Condensation: two monomer types
alternating, and a small molecule — water here, hydrogen
chloride elsewhere — expelled at every junction. Add the
functional groups and the two routes cannot be confused:
addition monomers carry C=C; condensation monomers carry two
reactive end groups (–OH and –COOH here) and no double bond at
all. If the question shows you a –COOH at both ends, the
answer is condensation, whatever else it shows.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you define [[condensation-polymerisation]] and name the
small molecule usually lost? Can you draw or describe the
block diagram with the acid as one box and the [[diol]] as the
other, water removed at every seam? Can you write the
structural formulae of ethane-1,2-diol and ethanedioic acid
and explain each code in their names? Can you reproduce the
balanced equation with 2n waters? If yes, the [[polyester]]
machinery is yours and the biodegradable members are next.
:::

sections.title: Biodegradable polyesters
sections.markdown:
Condensation polymers carry a different environmental account
from the addition polymers of the disposal section, and the
difference traces back to their seams. As with addition
polymers there are environmental issues with the disposal of
condensation polymers, but these are more reactive because of
the ester linkage in the chain, and they will
all break down eventually — although "eventually" can still
mean hundreds of years. The ester groups give the bacteria's
chemistry somewhere to attack. Building on that crack in the
armour, scientists have developed some biodegradable
[[polyester]]s which break down much more quickly. These are
called [[biopolyester]]s, and they are the closest thing this
chapter offers to a solution of the disposal problem that
addition polymers created.

The flagship [[biopolyester]] is made from lactic acid. Lactic
acid can be obtained from corn starch, and when it undergoes
polymerisation it forms a biodegradable polyester —
[[polylactic-acid]], or PLA — which can be used for making
biodegradable plastic bags or in surgery for internal
stitches. Both uses lean on the same property: the material
does its job, then quietly goes away. A compostable bag
decomposes with the compost; a suture holds the wound while it
heals and then degrades inside the body without a second
operation to remove it.

:::did-you-know
Lactic acid, more properly known as 2-hydroxypropanoic acid
(CH₃CHOHCOOH), has both an alcohol group and a carboxylic acid
group in the same molecule — so it can polymerise with itself.
One molecule supplies both ends of every condensation join,
which is why a single monomer type is enough to build PLA.
:::

:::cross-curricular
The amino-acid extension of condensation polymerisation is the
chemistry behind biology's most important polymers. Amino
acids carry an amine group (–NH₂) and a carboxylic acid group
(–COOH) in the same molecule; the amine group reacts very
similarly to the –OH group of alcohols, connecting with a
carboxylic acid to form an amide bond. When amino acids join
together this way they form polypeptides — the primary
structure of every protein, from enzymes to keratin. The
condensation logic you learned in the previous section is,
literally, the logic of you.
:::

:::exam-hint
Statement 4.50C is a *know*: some polyesters, known as
[[biopolyester]]s, are biodegradable. The examinable chain is
short — condensation polymers are more reactive than addition
polymers because of the ester linkage; biopolyesters break
down much more quickly; PLA is made from lactic acid obtained
from corn starch. A one-mark question usually wants the
linkage; a two-mark question wants the linkage *and* the
consequence. Do not overclaim: ordinary condensation polymers
also break down eventually — hundreds of years — so
"biodegradable" means faster, not instant.
:::

:::misconception
"Biodegradable means the plastic disappears in days in any
bin or sea." The word is comparative, not magical. Ordinary
condensation polymers already break down eventually — their
ester links are attackable — but that can take hundreds of
years, and [[polylactic-acid]] still needs the right
conditions to decompose usefully. What the [[biopolyester]]
label promises is *much more quickly*, not overnight, and
never a licence for littering.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you explain why condensation polymers are more reactive
than addition polymers, naming the linkage responsible? Can
you name a [[biopolyester]], its monomer, where that monomer
comes from, and two uses? Can you say what makes lactic acid
able to polymerise with itself? If yes, every statement of
this chapter has been taught and the question bank is next.
:::

sections.title: Chapter 29 questions
sections.markdown:
You now hold the complete synthetic-polymers story. The
addition half: alkenes open their C=C bonds and add on, an initiator starting chains of 4000 to 40 000 carbons, with
nothing lost (4.44); the repeat-unit routine runs forwards for
poly(ethene), poly(propene), PVC and PTFE (4.45) and
backwards from any drawn polymer to its monomer (4.46); and
the disposal bill follows from the chemistry — strong covalent
bonds make the [[polymer]] inert and non-biodegradable, and
burning it trades landfill for carbon dioxide and toxic gases
(4.47). The condensation half, Paper 2C only: a diol and a
dicarboxylic acid alternate down a chain, water expelled at
every seam, an ester link at every junction (4.48C); the
repeat unit and balanced equation for the ethanedioic acid +
ethane-1,2-diol polyester (4.49C); and the biopolyesters,
PLA from lactic acid, that break down far faster than their
addition cousins (4.50C). Two equations anchor the chapter —
the ethene-to-poly(ethene) addition and the
diol-plus-dioic-acid condensation with its 2n waters — and one
routine runs the whole show: open the double bond going in,
restore it coming out.

Every specification statement of this chapter — 4.44 to 4.50C —
has been taught, and each now joins the platform question bank
through the links below, with practice items keyed to exactly
those statements.

Before opening the bank, rehearse the shapes the
questions wear. The addition half asks for terms defined
precisely (unsaturated, hydrocarbon, polymerisation, addition),
a balanced combustion equation for ethene, displayed formulae
and three-repeat-unit chain diagrams, the styrene
polymerisation with the C₆H₅ group carried whole, and the
monomer decode behind a Perspex-style chain fragment — the
4.46 routine run on unfamiliar furniture. The decision question
asks you to take a side on landfill versus incineration and
defend it with two reasons from the trade-off table. The
condensation half, Paper 2C only, asks you to identify a
polyester from a block diagram and draw its monomers, to build
a PET/Terylene chain two repeat units long with its balanced
equation from ethane-1,2-diol and terephthalic acid, and to
extend the whole pattern to nylon — diamine plus dioic acid,
amide links instead of ester links, the same remove-water
logic. Shapes, not scripts: every one of them is answered by
the routines already in your hands.

:::exam-hint
Read every bank question with the paper route in mind: the
addition-polymer items can reach you on Paper 1C as well as
2C, while anything asking for a polyester, a PET chain or a
nylon block diagram is C-suffixed territory — Paper 2C only.
And when a question shows a polymer fragment you have never
seen, that is not a new topic: it is the 4.46 routine wearing
a costume, so find two adjacent chain carbons and put the
double bond back.
:::

:::misconception
"The final chapter must be the hardest, so polymer questions
are where to expect defeat." This chapter is the most
procedural of the organic set: nearly every mark traces back
to one drawing routine read forwards or backwards, one
balanced condensation equation, and one trade-off argument
you have already written out. Difficulty in polymer questions
comes from unfamiliar drawings, not unfamiliar chemistry —
and the routine dissolves unfamiliarity on contact.
:::

:::quick-check
Can you still draw all four named addition repeat units from
memory, with continuation bonds and the subscript n? Can you
write the polyester equation unprompted and say where the
2n waters came from? Can you give the disposal argument in
examiner's terms — inertness, non-biodegradability, toxic
gases? If yes, walk into the bank; every statement in it has
a section of this lesson behind it.
:::

:::summary
Addition polymerisation joins many small alkene [[monomer]]s
into one giant molecule with nothing expelled; the
[[repeat-unit]] sits in square brackets with continuation
bonds crossing the walls and a subscript n. The routine runs
forwards from any alkene (ethene, propene, chloroethene,
tetrafluoroethene) and backwards from any polymer to its
monomer. The chains are saturated, inert and
non-biodegradable, so disposal is landfill versus incineration
with real trade-offs on both sides. [[condensation-polymerisation]]
alternates two monomers — a diol and a
dicarboxylic acid — expelling water at every junction and
building [[polyester]] chains stitched by ester links; its
equation balances with 2n waters per n repeat units. Because
the ester links are attackable, condensation polymers break
down eventually, and the biopolyesters — PLA from corn-starch
lactic acid — break down much faster.
:::

:::can-you
Draw the addition equation for any named alkene and the
backwards monomer decode for any drawn polymer? State why
poly(ethene) will not decolourise bromine water and why that
same fact is its disposal problem? Give both sides of both
disposal routes and name the toxic gases? Draw the polyester
repeat unit from the two monomers, balance the equation with
2n H₂O, and say which statements of the chapter are Paper 2C
only? If every answer is yes, the chapter — and the organic
chemistry of this specification — is complete.
:::
